metadata.title: General or specific abilities? Evidence from 33 countries participating in the PISA assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 public-use files and states that, with appropriate weights, the PISA samples are representative of 15-year-olds in participating OECD countries. PISA sampling is described as a two-stage stratified design (schools stratified, then students randomly selected within sampled schools), which implies the need for complex-sample weighting when estimating population-representative parameters. The paper does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT) or whether weights were applied in the reported model-fitting and SEM steps, so the exact weighting implementation cannot be verified from the provided text. The analytic sample is further restricted by excluding Spain (reading administration problems) and using a subsample for Canada due to computational constraints.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the study does not use PV-based achievement scores as dependent variables; instead, it estimates latent ability factors from item-level responses using IRT/CFA-style measurement models. Missing data handling is described via full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in the covariate SEM stage, which is treated as multiple imputation in this schema mapping. Therefore, PV handling does not apply to the latent-factor modeling approach used here, while missingness is addressed through FIML rather than PV-based imputation or deletion.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2018 public-use files and restricts analyses to OECD countries and to computer-based assessment administrations (all OECD countries implemented the test on computer). Spain is excluded due to problems with the administration of the reading assessment in 2018. For Canada, a random subsample of 12,994 students is used because the full sample (22,653) was too large for the computations required. The reported total sample size (226,434 students) applies to the major domain (reading); sample sizes for the minor domains (mathematics and science) are smaller, consistent with PISA rotation/adaptive design and incomplete balanced matrix administration.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (major domain), OECD countries (33 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Model fit: general-ability bifactor vs multidimensional vs S-1 reading bifactor
main_findings.performance_metrics: AIC: symmetrical bifactor model has the smallest AIC in all 33 countries; ΔAIC (symmetrical bifactor vs 3D) > 100 in 30/33 countries; ΔAIC (symmetrical bifactor vs S-1) > 150 in 32/33 countries (United States exception: 110).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data from 33 OECD countries, the study compared three psychometric measurement models (multidimensional, symmetrical bifactor with general ability, and S-1 reading bifactor) and found that the symmetrical bifactor model produced the best fit by AIC in all countries, with very large ΔAIC differences versus the other models. This indicates that PISA item responses are largely structured by a general ability factor rather than by distinct domain-specific reading, mathematics, and science factors, informing assessment design and interpretation of domain scores.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (major domain), OECD countries (33 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Discriminant validity of domain factors in the multidimensional model
main_findings.performance_metrics: Factor correlations (3D model): reading–mathematics > 0.8 in all 33 countries; mathematics–science generally > 0.8 and sometimes > 0.90; reading–science generally between the other two correlations; discriminant validity judged poor because all but one between-factor correlation exceeds 0.8.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data from 33 OECD countries, the study estimated correlations among the three domain factors in the standard multidimensional model and found consistently very high inter-domain correlations (mostly > 0.8), implying poor discriminant validity. This indicates that the conventional domain-specific constructs in PISA scaling are heavily contaminated by a shared general factor, suggesting caution when using domain scores to infer distinct domain-specific competencies.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (major domain), OECD countries (33 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Reliability and explained common variance of specific factors in the symmetrical bifactor model
main_findings.performance_metrics: Symmetrical bifactor indices: ECV for general factor around ≥0.8; average specific-factor ECVSS (common variance in subdomain items beyond general): mathematics 0.27, science 0.17, reading 0.12. Omega hierarchical (ωH) > 0.8 in all countries (unit-weighted total scores essentially unidimensional). Average omega subscale confounding: reading specific reliable variance ≈ 5% (0.044/0.982), mathematics ≈ 24% (0.221/0.938), science ≈ 14% (0.135/0.952).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data from 33 OECD countries, the study quantified bifactor reliability and explained common variance and found that the general factor accounts for the vast majority of common variance (ECV around 0.8+), while specific-factor contributions are small—especially for reading and science—and ωH exceeds 0.8 everywhere. This indicates that domain-specific subscores derived from the symmetrical bifactor structure have low incremental reliability, implying that policy and research should not over-interpret domain score differences as reflecting distinct domain abilities.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (major domain), OECD countries (33 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Covariate relationships with latent factors (gender, ESCS, learning time)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Standardized SEM coefficients summarized by country boxplots: ESCS effects average ~0.26 in the multidimensional model and ~0.25 in the general-ability bifactor model; ESCS not significantly associated with reading and science in most countries under the general-ability bifactor, and only weakly associated with mathematics. Under the S-1 reading model, ESCS is moderately correlated with reading (~0.26) but weakly with mathematics and science. Learning time patterns: language-of-test learning time shows negative relationships with reading in multidimensional and reading-bifactor models; effects in bifactor general model are generally positive but very small; mathematics learning time effects are close to zero; science learning time is more strongly associated with reading in multidimensional and S-1 models but has no relationship with reading in the bifactor model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data from 33 OECD countries, the study estimated SEM relationships between gender, ESCS, learning time and latent factors and found that ESCS and gender patterns align more with general cognitive ability than with domain-specific expectations, while learning-time associations are weak or counter-theoretical in several models. This indicates that ex post interpretations of PISA domain scores using background covariates may largely reflect general ability structure, so interventions targeting domain-specific learning time may require more precise measurement frameworks.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 item-level responses from 33 OECD countries (total N=226,434 for the major reading domain) to test whether PISA primarily measures general ability or distinct domain-specific abilities. The authors compare three psychometric measurement models—(i) a standard three-dimensional correlated-factor model, (ii) a symmetrical bifactor model with a general ability factor, and (iii) an S-1 bifactor reading model—using AIC for model fit and bifactor indices (ECV, ω, ωH, and omega subscale coefficients) for reliability and explained common variance. The symmetrical bifactor model yields the best fit in all countries with very large ΔAIC differences, and the general factor explains most common variance (ECV around 0.8+), while specific-factor contributions are small and often too unreliable for interpretable domain subscores. Covariate SEM results show ESCS and gender relationships consistent with general ability, and learning-time effects are weak or sometimes counter to theoretical expectations. Limitations include reliance on latent-factor modeling rather than PV-based achievement scores and the use of FIML for missingness, without reporting a PV-handling strategy.
